body.text: On October 23, the Central Bank of Uzbekistan (CBU) issued its first license granting official permission to provide Islamic banking services to Open Bank Joint-Stock Company, marking a new page in the country’s attempt to expand financial inclusion.

Uzbekistan has been trying to expand access to financial services and bring more money into the formal banking system for years. In 2019, Uzbekistan became a member of the International Islamic Trade and Finance Corporation and the Investment and Export Credit Insurance Islamic Corporation.

President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, in his 2020 address to the parliament, highlighted the need to introduce Islamic financing. “The time has come to create a legal framework for the introduction of Islamic financial services in our country,” Mirziyoyev said. “Experts from the Islamic Development Bank and other international financial organizations will be involved in this regard.”

In a 2023 pre-election meeting with potential voters in Namangan, one of the most populated areas of Uzbekistan historically following a stricter form of Islam, Mirziyoyev even promised to have Islamic financing system operating in Namangan.

Although Uzbekistan allowed microfinance organizations to provide Islamic financing from 2022, the CBU only approved regulations governing such services in 2024. That year, the CBU joined the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB). In 2025, Tashkent hosted the 20th International Shariah Scholars Forum in Islamic Finance (ISSF) – the first time the event was held outside Malaysia.
Also in 2024, the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis adopted a draft law on introducing Islamic banking activities.

In 2026, progress accelerated. In March, Mirziyoyev signed a law that established the legal framework for organizing Islamic banking, including establishing licensing, regulating, and taxing requirements. By mid-July, the CBU established a Islamic Finance Council of five people, including members from the Muslim Board of Uzbekistan.
While Tashkent’s ambitions are clear, the economic case rests on two expectations: that people use Islamic financing and savers will place their savings in Islamic investment accounts.

Uzbekistan is a Muslim-majority country with a total population exceeding 39 million. The exact number of Muslims is hard to gauge – while both the U.S. Department of State and Human Rights Watch estimate that over 80 percent of the population follow Islam, the Committee on Religious Affairs of Uzbekistan reported that figure to be 94 percent as of 2015. Neither, however, estimates how many Uzbek citizens would prefer Islamic financing, regardless of their faith.

In 2023, Bakhrom Nomonov, then chairman of the board of Apex Bank, noted that 20 percent of Uzbek citizens do not take out traditional loans from banks due to their religious beliefs. Therefore, he argued, Islamic financing could attract up to $10 billion a year to the country. A 2020 survey conducted within the framework of the United Nations Development Program on “Analysis of Islamic financial products in Uzbekistan” also indicated religious beliefs as one of the main reasons many Uzbek people not to take out traditional bank loans.

The Muslim Board of Uzbekistan, as well as popular imams, all interpret riba – taking an interest-based loan from a bank (locally known as taking a credit) – as a sinful act, while other forms of Islamic financing – such as leasing, and murabaha –are deemed permissible.

This, however, does not mean a nationwide strict observation of Islam, including in finance. Many Uzbeks consider Islam a part of their culture. It is something that they are born into and many people simply do not follow every single fatwa or recommendation from an imam. (Uzbekistan is a secular state and the fatwas issued by imams are not binding by law.) The existence of some strict observers is matched by those with more lax approaches. The latest report from the Central Bank shows that as of 2025, 20 percent of adults in the country have an active bank credit account with almost one-third of them having taken 1.7 loans on average.

Whether Uzbek citizens take out bank loans or put their savings into investment accounts is not entirely – or even predominantly – a religious question. The availability of halal loans might create more chances, but if Islamic financing costs more than conventional bank loans – when a new product is launched, it usually competes with other similar products in the market – there is no guarantee that the Muslims of Uzbekistan will choose a more expensive halal one.

Another obstacle lies with reputation. Inclusion of members from the Muslim Board of Uzbekistan into the CBU’s Islamic Finance Council will increase its credibility among the public as the majority of Muslims in Uzbekistan trust official religious endorsements. However, this also raises the question of who checks these systems for compliance and conducts audits. IMAN invest, a company that offers Islamic investment products, is currently embroiled in a huge scandal. The Islamic Finance Consulting Board (IFCB) terminated its cooperation with the company, with board member Mahmud Usmon alleging misuse of investor funds in violation of Islamic finance principles and a deficit of $20 million in its investment portfolio. The company has disputed the allegation and is trying to restore public trust.

This one dispute does not mean that licensed Islamic banks will face the same difficulties or allegations, but the risks remain. It just takes one respected scholar questioning a product’s Islamic compliance to undermine public trust, and without public trust even the devout might shy away from Islamic financing options.

Reportedly, more than 10 commercial banks in Uzbekistan are preparing to introduce Islamic finance products. Their success with previously underserved populations is to be seen in the coming years and is subject to competing services and credibility. The number of licenses is an initial indicator of interest, not a guarantee of success.
